scenario.label: Rebuilding the payments integration
scenario.brief: We are replacing the payments integration in eight weeks. Before anybody writes code I want each person to say what they think the scope is, what they are waiting on, and what they think will go wrong. I have been burned by a project where everybody agreed at the start and nobody had the same thing in their head.
scenario.theDecision: The engineer and the ops lead have different scopes: one is replacing the gateway only, the other assumes reconciliation is included, which is three extra weeks. Nobody has priced the reconciliation work. A right answer names the scope difference as the first thing to settle, not the timeline.

people.name: Ifeoma Chukwu
people.remit: Head of engineering. Owns the eight-week deadline.
people.truth: She promised the board eight weeks. She believes the job is swapping the gateway and nothing else. She has not read the reconciliation requirement that finance sent in July. She has one engineer on it and no buffer.
people.manner: Crisp, deadline-focused. Gives dates readily. Slightly defensive about the eight weeks.

people.name: Samuel Otieno
people.truth: He has scoped the gateway swap at five weeks and is confident. He has seen the finance reconciliation document and assumed somebody else was handling it. He is waiting on sandbox credentials from the provider, requested eleven days ago, no reply. He has not told Ifeoma about the credentials because he thinks it will resolve itself.
people.manner: Understated. Gives precise technical detail. Does not escalate. Says "should be fine" until pressed.

people.name: Rita Adeleke
people.truth: She sent the reconciliation requirement in July and got no reply. Her team reconciles 400 transactions by hand every morning and the whole point of the rebuild, for her, is that this stops. If it is not in scope the project is worthless to her. She assumes it is in scope because nobody told her otherwise.
people.manner: Practical, a bit weary, very specific about volumes and time taken.

turns.text: This conversation is about getting everyone clear on the payments integration project, which you kicked off. What do you see as the core objective that needs to exist at the end of this payments integration project?
The core objective is to replace our current payments gateway. We need to be fully switched over.
To make sure that's clear, what specific capabilities will this new gateway need to have that the old one didn't, or that it improves upon?
suggestedAnswers: We know the key new capabilities.
We are still figuring that out.
That is next on our list.

turns.text: This project is about swapping out the gateway. It's a like-for-like replacement. We are not adding new capabilities in this phase.
Understood. A like, for-like replacement means the focus is on a seamless transition, rather than new features. What do you see as the biggest challenge in making that switch seamless?
suggestedAnswers: I think it will be seamless.
The biggest challenge is the ... migration.
I haven't thought about it yet.

turns.text: The biggest challenge will be ensuring the cutover happens smoothly on the technical side. We need to minimize any disruption to transactions.
Minimizing disruption on the technical side during cutover is key. Is there anything you need that's blocked on someone else right now for this to happen?
suggestedAnswers: I am waiting on technical support.

turns.text: No, not right now. We have an engineer assigned to it. I'm not waiting on anything specific to get started.
For this payments integration, what is your planned approach for getting it off the check-in?
suggestedAnswers: Engineer started. We have a plan.
Still need a clear path forward.
I don't know the approach yet.

turns.text: We'll define the technical requirements, develop the integration, and then thoroughly test it. The deadline is eight weeks from now.
Eight weeks from now. What aspects of this project are currently clear to you?
The scope is clear: replace the payment gateway. The deadline is clear: eight weeks. We have an engineer ready to go.
You also said the focus is a seamless transition. What would you need to see, specifically, to know the cutover had been seamless?
suggestedAnswers: I'd see payments processing without issues.
I'm still figuring out what to watch.

turns.text: I'd need to see zero downtime for payments and all transactions processing correctly through the new gateway. No customer impact, basically.
Beyond the immediate project team, who has a stake in this, and what do you understand they expect?
suggestedAnswers: I know who the stakeholders are.
I haven't talked to them yet.

turns.text: The board has a stake; they expect it done in eight weeks. Finance will be using the new system, of course, but their main concern is usually just that it works.

You've named the board and Finance as key stakeholders. You also mentioned "no customer impact" as a measure of a seamless cutover. Whose records would show whether there was customer impact, or whether all transactions processed correctly?
Our internal transaction logs and customer support feedback would show customer impact. Finance would verify if all transactions processed correctly.

That gives us clear sources for verifying the customer impact and transaction processing. Now, you set up this check-in to get everyone clear on the project's scope, dependencies, and risks. This is the first session, so what have you decided to do about this payments integration, and by when?
suggestedAnswers: I have a plan for the integration by ...
I am still stuck on a few things.
I have not decided what to do yet.

turns.text: Before anything else, so this asks you the right things: are you the person this check-in is about, or somebody working alongside them? One line is enough.
I am Samuel Otieno, the senior engineer. I'm doing the build for this integration.
Understood. What did you understand your role in this project to be, in your own words?
suggestedAnswers: My role is to build the integration.
I did not fully understand my role.
I am still clarifying my understanding of my role.

turns.text: I'm leading the technical implementation of the new payments integration. My role is to make sure the swap happens smoothly.

I need to understand the problem better first.

turns.text: First, I need to get access to the sandbox environment. I can't start coding until I have that.

I'm waiting on the sandbox credentials from the provider. I requested them eleven days ago.

No, there is nothing in writing yet.
I don't know, I need to check.

turns.text: Yes, I have the email I sent requesting the credentials.

I don't see any problems yet.

turns.text: My role is to make sure the new integration handles the daily reconciliation process correctly.
What specifically exists as a definition for "correctly" here?
"Correctly" means it automates the reconciliation of the 400 transactions my team currently does by hand every morning.

Four hundred transactions currently done by hand each morning. What would success look like for that automation, what would exist that doesn't exist today if that is genuinely delivered? For instance, a daily report from the new system, or a notification that confirms all 400 transactions have been reconciled without manual intervention.
Success would be a daily automated report that confirms the 400 transactions are reconciled. No manual work.
That daily report confirming all 400 transactions are reconciled without manual work sounds like a clear outcome. What do you think is most likely to go wrong with getting that built and running?
suggestedAnswers: The data might not reconcile easily.
Integrating all systems could be hard.

turns.text: I think the biggest risk is that the reconciliation requirement gets overlooked, or assumed to be out of scope.

You think the biggest risk is that the reconciliation requirement gets overlooked, or assumed to be out of scope. That is the kind of thing that stalls a project in the middle.
